transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-11-07
Start: 14:00 PT | Duration ~58 minutes
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Noah (Redwood SE), Elena (CISO), Raj (Head Infra), Priya (Cloud Security), Liam (Network)

Summary:
Quick technical/legal sync focused on private deployment hardening: control-plane egress, ingress controls, firewalling, KMS integration and audit logging requirements for SOC2/ISO posture. Customer emphasized strict data residency and desire for deterministic egress for outbound telemetry.

Topics:
- Control plane vs data-plane network flows
- Egress allowlist / egress proxy options (HTTP proxy, TLS-inspecting forward proxy concerns)
- Private VPC endpoints, NAT and air-gapped operations
- KMS/HSM patterns and key rotation, BYOK considerations
- Audit logs, SIEM forwarding, retention and tamper-proofing
- RBAC/SSO (SAML, SCIM) and separation of duties for control plane access

Action items (recorded in metadata above).

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan: okay hey everyone thanks for making time, we'll try to keep this focused on the network and the controls you called out in the questionnaire. um Maya and Noah from our infra team are with me. Elena, do you want to kick us off with the high-level constraints?
[00:12] Elena: sure, right. thanks Jordan. um so two quick bullets: one, all logs and PII-derived artifacts for EU customers must stay in our eu-central region; second, outbound network egress from the private deployment is tightly controlled — we use an allowlist via an egress proxy and we cannot have unexpected third-party telemetry going out.
[00:29] Raj: and to add, we have a strict airgap option for some regulated workloads where no direct outbound is allowed, only an approved pull mechanism. we want to understand how Redwood's control plane communicates in that scenario.
[00:40] Maya: great, thanks. quick clarification: when you say control plane, you mean Redwood's management/control traffic (version updates, health checks, metrics) versus the model inference data plane, correct?
[00:49] Priya: yeah that's right. we want model requests to stay local to our VPC, but the control plane sometimes phones home for metrics and licensing checks — those are the ones we need mapped.
[00:58] Noah: okay good, so at a high level Redwood private can be deployed with an "isolated control plane" option where the control plane either sits in the customer's VPC or connects to a private endpoint. there are three primary patterns: 1) fully local control plane (on-prem), 2) control plane in customer VPC with private endpoints to Redwood management, and 3) managed control plane with egress via a customer-managed egress proxy. each has different implications for firewall rules and KMS.
[01:20] Liam: when you say private endpoints, do you support AWS PrivateLink or equivalent for GCP/azure? we can't punch 443 to the public internet.
[01:28] Maya: yes we support PrivateLink and Private Service Connect patterns. in that config the control plane traffic is over private connectivity — you can lock security groups to only allow that. there is still metadata sync that may require outbound TLS to certain domains if you choose the managed-control-plane route.
[01:42] Raj: how deterministic is that outbound list? we need to put it in our firewall allowlist and our change control process.
[01:48] Jordan: we maintain a published egress domain list for managed control plane and for telemetry. we'll share a current snapshot. we try to keep that stable, but there are occasional additions for telemetry endpoints.
[01:58] Elena: any chance we can configure the telemetry to be pulled (pull model) instead of phone-home? pull is easier for our auditors.
[02:05] Maya: yes, there is an option for periodic pull via an approved staging bucket or S3-compatible endpoint that the Redwood control plane will poll for updates rather than sending outbound. that's often used for airgap scenarios. it's more manual but passes auditors' requirements.
[02:20] Priya: about KMS — our policy requires keys be in an HSM-backed KMS and keys must never leave eu region. can you support a BYOK flow and on-prem HSM?
[02:29] Noah: short answer: yes. Redwood supports both cloud KMS integrations and HSMs through a KMIP-like interface or customer-managed HSMs. we have a BYOK onboarding flow that can integrate with Thales/Entrust or cloud HSMs. keys can be configured to stay in-region, and we support enveloping — model payloads are encrypted with a local data key that is itself wrapped by your KMS.
[02:48] Raj: do you do any caching of keys in the control plane? that's a red flag for us.
[02:52] Maya: we use short-lived key material caches only within the inference runtime to avoid latency hits, but the long-term keys are always retrieved from KMS with enforced TTL and we can place them behind HSM. we can also show the exact TTL and cache invalidation in the onboarding docs.
[03:07] Elena: and rotation? we need automated rotation every 90 days and full audit trail of key usage.
[03:12] Noah: rotation is supported; we can rotate and rewrap data keys non-disruptively. we also emit key-usage logs to the audit log stream so your SIEM can pick it up.
[03:20] Priya: about audit logs — we need append-only retention for 7 years for certain workloads and tamper evidence. can Redwood forward to our SIEM (we use Splunk) without sending a copy to Redwood-managed long-term storage?
[03:33] Maya: yes, logs can be streamed to customer-managed endpoints via TLS to your ingest. options: direct syslog/TLS, FluentD/FluentBit forwarding, or a push to an S3 bucket under your control. we don't keep a copy unless you opt-in — default is to forward only.
[03:48] Liam: if we forward over TLS, do you do certificate pinning or mTLS? we have strict MITM threat model.
[03:55] Maya: we support client TLS with mutual TLS for log forwarding and can do cert pinning. we can also support signed envelopes for log events to provide tamper evidence.
[04:05] Raj: firewall rules — what are the exact ports and IPs needed for the control plane? we need to model the firewall and NAT for the whole cluster.
[04:13] Noah: short list: control plane uses 443/TCP for API endpoints; internal cluster heartbeats may use high ephemeral ports depending on the runtime (we'll give a definitive list). for managed-control-plane deployments you only need to allow outbound 443 to the published domains or to the PrivateLink endpoints. if you use the egress proxy pattern, we'll be able to point to a single host and port.
[04:32] Priya: can we run TLS inspection at the egress proxy? our DLP team sometimes wants that but we have concerns about cert interception and Redwood's signing requirements.
[04:40] Maya: we recommend avoiding TLS interception for model payloads because we do end-to-end TLS and the runtime detects tampering; interception can break client certificate validation. for metadata/telemetry you could inspect, but we'd prefer mTLS or an allowlist at the proxy.
[04:55] Elena: auditors also ask about RBAC and SSO — we want separation of duties: operators can run jobs but can't change KMS policies or export keys. how is admin split between Redwood control plane admin and customer IAM?
[05:05] Jordan: Redwood supports role-based access with fine-grained roles. for private deployments you can map Redwood roles to your IdP via SAML plus SCIM for provisioning. we also support a model where the control plane's root admin is in your SSO and Redwood technical contacts are invited as operators with limited scopes.
[05:21] Priya: is there an audit trail for role changes? we need to see who added/removed roles and timestamped evidence.
[05:27] Maya: yes — all admin actions are logged and we can push those audit events to your SIEM. events include who (subject), action, target resource, before/after state and timestamp.
[05:38] Raj: regarding data residency, if we pin a model to eu-central and run inference in-region, can any telemetry accidentally leak to us-east for benchmarking or fallback?
[05:48] Noah: by design no — if you pin model and data residency, we route inference to in-region hosts only. fallback policies can be disabled; we can guarantee no cross-region fallback in the SLA for those accounts.
[05:58] Liam: ok but what about external third-party lib calls? we've seen other runtimes phone home for license checks to CDNs.
[06:05] Maya: good callout. we sandbox third-party tooling and do not allow arbitrary outbound flows from runtime containers. license checks for embedded components, if any, are part of the control-plane decision and included in the egress list we will provide.
[06:18] Elena: one nuance — our compliance team requires tamper-proof audit of the control plane itself. are there hard guarantees about immutability of configs?
[06:25] Noah: we have config change logs with signed checkpoints. in private deploy we can optionally store signed config snapshots in your object store. that gives you immutability guarantees and provenance.
[06:35] Jordan: quick question from us — what timeline are you targeting for POC? and which workloads are in-scope?
[06:41] Raj: initial POC is two EU-regulated models in a private VPC, low throughput, but must meet SOC2 controls. timeline is Q1 2028 for a pilot; procurement wants technical sign-off by end of November.
[06:52] Jordan: helpful. we'll prioritize the audit docs and the network diagram then.
[06:56] Priya: about SOC2 evidence — do you have a packaged artifact set for on-prem customers or is the SOC2 report only covering hosted?
[07:03] Maya: our SOC2 Type II covers both hosted and private deployment patterns; we also provide a private-deploy checklist that maps controls to artifacts you can collect from your side (e.g., KMS rotation logs, SIEM forward confirmations). we'll share the matrix.
[07:15] Elena: any third-party pentest results? we need to see recent vuln scans.
[07:20] Noah: yes, we run quarterly pentests and can share redacted reports under NDA.
[07:25] Raj: circling back to NAT and egress — what's the recommended pattern for customers who disallow outbound DNS resolution to public resolvers? we use internal resolvers and we want to avoid recursive DNS to the internet.
[07:35] Maya: you can configure the control plane to use your VPC DNS, and we can also accept endpoint IPs rather than hostnames for firewall rules if needed. for managed-control-plane we support VPC endpoints and private DNS mapping so you don't need public DNS resolution.
[07:49] Liam: on firewall logs — do you provide correlation IDs on outgoing requests so we can match firewall logs to Redwood events? that helps incident investigations.
[07:57] Noah: yes, we can surface hop-by-hop correlation IDs. runtime emits a request id header X-Redwood-Req-Id and we include that in audit events so you can stitch logs together.
[08:07] Priya: question on signing — do you sign log streams? we want to ensure logs forwarded to our SIEM haven't been tampered before arrival.
[08:14] Maya: we can sign batches of events with a key you control or with a Redwood signing key and provide an attestation. for highest assurance we recommend pushing to a customer-controlled S3 bucket with server-side immutability (e.g., object lock) and then pulling from there into SIEM.
[08:29] Elena: what about emergency revoke of keys or shutting down a control plane quickly in case of compromise?
[08:35] Noah: we provide an emergency kill switch for customer-controlled deployments: a single API call or a console toggle (backed by SSO MFA) that will isolate the control plane and revoke runtime certs. we can support an airgap lockdown script as part of runbooks.
[08:50] Jordan: that sounds good. any other regulatory specifics for ISO?
[08:54] Priya: ISO auditors will want documented change management and evidence of separation of duties — those are the RBAC and signed config snapshots we discussed.
[09:02] Maya: yep, we'll include that mapping in the artifact matrix.
[09:08] Elena: one last operational note: our SOC team wants to validate Redwood's ability to meet retention and egress SLAs. can we run a short integration where we send sample events to our SIEM and validate chain-of-custody?
[09:19] Noah: absolutely — that's a simple forwarder config and we'll help you validate signatures and timestamps.
[09:25] Raj: timeline again: can you get the network diagram and the egress list by next week? procurement will probably want to feed that into the firewall change window.
[09:33] Jordan: yes, Maya will produce that by Wednesday.
[09:36] Maya: noted. I'll include both PrivateLink endpoint details, IP ranges, and a conservative allowlist plus notes for the airgap pull flow.
[09:45] Priya: on KMS rotation and audit — will you publish a sample CloudTrail log schema for key usage events? we want to ingest into Splunk parsers.
[09:54] Noah: we will produce a sample schema and Splunk HEC example.
[09:58] Elena: okay great. any outstanding blockers?
[10:01] Liam: nothing technical here other than verifying the IP list and mTLS options.
[10:05] Raj: and procurement wants a statement of no data residency crossing — can that be added to the pilot contract?
[10:11] Jordan: yes we can add a clause for the pilot. we'll loop in legal after this call.
[10:15] Maya: small gotcha to note: if you enable advanced telemetry (debug-level), some debug logs may include hashed request fragments — we advise to keep debug off for regulated workloads.
[10:25] Priya: good to know. we'll disable debug and only enable info level for POC.
[10:30] Jordan: ok wrapping up — we'll share artifacts, SOC2, pentest summary under NDA and schedule the on-prem walkthrough. who will own the schedule from Stonehaven?
[10:40] Elena: Priya and Liam will coordinate dates and Raj will sign off on the firewall changes.
[10:44] Jordan: great. thanks everyone. we'll follow up with a recording, the diagrams, and the action list.
[10:49] (end of recorded discussion)
